notes:
I've written notes for part of 1 Peter 1, not all of it. The research tools hit a hard usage limit early, and after that I couldn't open any pages in full. The notes below come only from the search-result excerpts I did get. That means good coverage of vv. 1–6, but only one or two older sources for vv. 7, 9–10, 12 and 21–23. **Nothing on vv. 8, 11, 13–20 or 24–25.** I also found nothing on modern scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox readings, or prosperity / word of faith / hyper-grace teaching, so those sections are left out.

One more caveat: Bible Hub's combined pages (biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-X.htm) often run several commentators' text together without saying who wrote what. Where an excerpt didn't name its author, I call it "an older commentator on that page" rather than guess.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- By calling himself an "apostle of Jesus Christ," Peter claims authority to speak for Christ. The readers lived in what is now Turkey, and scholars argue a lot about whether they were Jewish or Gentile believers. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-peter/
- One older commentator takes "the dispersion of Pontus" to mean Jews scattered among the Gentiles, by comparison with John 7:35. On this view the home being contrasted is Palestine, not heaven, and Peter, apostle to the Jews, is writing to Jewish Christians. The same page has MacLaren noting that the Revised Version reads "sojourners of the Dispersion." He sees Jewish ideas being carried over to Christians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-1.htm
- Barclay says "Diaspora" was the technical name for Jews living outside Palestine. Now, he says, the real Diaspora is the Church spread across the empire: exiles whose home is eternity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/1-peter-1.html
- Gann thinks Nero's persecution may have driven Christians into these provinces. Chuck Smith notes that "scattered" comes from the Greek word for dispersing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/1-1.html

**v. 2**
- One older commentator: the election was individual, not just of the group. But he says it means God put these people into the visible Church, and does not make them certain of salvation. The verse links election to all three Persons of the Trinity: its origin (the Father's foreknowledge), its aim, and its means. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-2.htm
- Chuck Smith sums the verse up as the Trinity working together: chosen by the Father, set apart by the Spirit, cleansed by Christ's blood. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/c2000_1Pe/1Pe_001.cfm
- Bible.org: one privilege of being chosen is a steady supply of God's grace and peace. https://bible.org/seriespage/1-privileges-election-1-peter-11-2
- The Biblical Illustrator: the "obedience" here is both the obedience of believing the gospel and the obedience faith produces. It also says Christ's blood works through faith, both to pay for sin and to put sin to death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-peter-1.html

**v. 3**
- Enduring Word (Guzik): "begotten us again" is worded differently from "born again" in John 3:3 but means the same thing, a new creation. The hope is "living" because believers share eternal life with a Saviour who beat death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-peter-1/
- Ellicott calls vv. 3–12 a hymn of praise for the gospel "from a Hebrew point of view." Another note on the same page ties our new birth back to Christ's resurrection. https://biblehub.com/1_peter/1-3.htm
- Spurgeon (quoted on Precept Austin) prefers "living" to "lively." Our first birth brought sin and sorrow; the second brings purity and joy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_13-5
- Piper names three foundations of the living hope: the new birth, God's great mercy, and Christ's resurrection. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-living-hope-through-the-resurrection-of-jesus-christ
- GotQuestions: a baby does nothing to get born, and neither do we. The "hope" here is assurance, not wishful thinking. https://www.gotquestions.org/living-hope.html
- One older commentator on Bible Hub: the resurrection proved Christ was God's Son, showed his sacrifice was accepted, and promises our own resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-3.htm

**v. 4**
- Calvin: the inheritance can't be destroyed by flood or fire. It is pure, unlike Canaan (the earthly picture of it), which its people defiled. And it doesn't fade, because this world is passing away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/1-4.html
- Older commentators on Bible Hub:
  - One says these readers had lost their inheritance in Palestine but have a better one waiting.
  - Another says heaven is what the Father gives his adopted children, and it could never corrupt the heart the way earthly riches can.
  - A third quotes Alford ("in substance incorruptible; in purity undefiled; in beauty unfading"). He notes the Greek tense of "reserved" means it is kept safe for good, out of Satan's reach.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-4.htm
- Wesley: "fadeth not away" means its worth never decays, unlike the leaf or flower crowns of ancient victors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm

**v. 5**
- Maclaren: the word is military ("guarded"). He pictures believers inside an army's hollow square, "guarded in the power of God." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/1-peter/by-through-unto.cfm
- GotQuestions: being kept doesn't spare believers from pain or hardship. https://www.gotquestions.org/kept-by-the-power-of-God.html
- BibleHub study notes: God's protection guards believers from final spiritual ruin, not from persecution or death. https://biblehub.com/1_peter/1-5.htm
- Clarke: the inheritance is guarded for Christ's true disciples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-peter-1.html

**v. 6**
- Clarke lists the options for what "wherein" refers to: the salvation, the last time, being kept, or all of the above. His view is that they rejoiced in their present salvation while looking ahead to the reward. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-peter-1.html
- Wesley:
  - "Wherein" means in being kept.
  - "If need be" means trials aren't always needed, only when God sees they help us spiritually.
  - The readers were sad but not "in darkness," since they still had faith, hope and love.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm

**v. 7**
- Wesley: "the trial of your faith" means your faith once it has been tested. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm

**v. 9**
- Wesley: "receiving" means now, already. The salvation is from all sin into all holiness, which prepares for and guarantees eternal salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html

**v. 10**
- Wesley: this salvation goes far beyond anything known under the Jewish system. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm

**v. 12**
- Wesley: the preaching was confirmed by the Holy Spirit's inner witness and his miraculous gifts. He sees a rising order of longing: prophets and kings wanted to see Christ's works, and now even angels long to understand what the Spirit taught about him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm

**v. 21**
- Wesley: all our faith and hope come from the power of Christ's resurrection, and God "glorified" him at the ascension. Without Christ we would only dread God; through him we believe, hope and love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html

**v. 22**
- Wesley: the Spirit freely gives both obedience and a pure heart. The call is to go on to "still higher degrees of love." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html

**v. 23**
- Wesley: the word "liveth" because it is full of divine power, and it stays the same forever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html
- Piper sets v. 3 beside v. 23. In v. 3 the new birth is purely God's miracle; in v. 23 it comes through a person hearing the word. He says the two can't be separated. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/born-again-by-the-book

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 1–2: what "elect according to foreknowledge" means**

*Reformed and Baptist: foreknowledge means God's prior love, not God looking ahead*
- MacArthur rejects the idea that God looked ahead, saw who would believe, and chose them. He reads "foreknew" as God loving his people before creation. https://gty.org/library/articles/A132/considering-election-not-politics
- Piper: "God foreknew me" means God recognised his own before the foundation of the world. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/divine-election-the-role-of-the-father-and-the-spirit
- Precept Austin quotes Wiersbe: if foreknowledge just meant God knew we'd believe, our salvation would be taken out of God's hands. It also quotes Spurgeon's picture of Election going ahead of Salvation and marking the houses it would visit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_12
- Sam Storms (Reformed and charismatic) says Peter doesn't shy away from election but proclaims it. Our rejection by the world comes from God having chosen us. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/remember-who-and-whose-you-are-1-peter-1:1-2
- Bible.org: choosing someone because God knew they'd accept him "makes God's choice not a choice at all." https://bible.org/seriespage/1-privileges-election-1-peter-11-2

*Methodist and Wesleyan*
- Wesley:
  - God has no "fore"-knowledge in the strict sense, since he sees everything as present; the word is God stooping to our level.
  - Election is God acting where our merit plays no part.
  - The true "predestination" is that whoever believes will be saved from sin, and whoever endures to the end will be saved eternally.
  - He sharply criticises the "modern predestinarian scheme." In his view it turns faith into a bare notion and Christ into a cover for sin rather than a Saviour from it.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/1_peter/1.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): if the letter were addressed to people elected to eternal life, nobody could have received it, because nobody could be sure of that election before reaching heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/acc/1-peter-1.html

*Calvary Chapel / non-Calvinist evangelical*
- Chuck Smith: God has always known who would respond to his grace, and on that basis chose them to be his children. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/smith_chuck/c2000_1Pe/1Pe_001.cfm

**v. 5: can believers fall away? ("kept... through faith")**

*Reformed, Puritan and Baptist*
- Thomas Watson: believers keep going in grace because of God's power. He notes that "Papists and Arminians" (his terms) oppose this doctrine. https://biblehub.com/study/1_peter/1-5.htm
- Precept Austin collects Barnes, Hawker, Winslow, Philpot and others. Their shared point: eternal security rests on God's faithfulness, not ours. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1_peter_15
- One older commentator on Bible Hub says the verse shows Peter, like Paul, held to the perseverance of the saints. Another lists ways believers are kept so they can never be separated from God, and says the faith itself will never fail. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-5.htm

*Wesleyan*
- Wesley: the inheritance is reserved and the heirs are kept for it, "through faith," by which salvation is both received and *retained*. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html
- One older commentator on Bible Hub: we are safe as long as we keep trusting. If faith failed altogether, we could not be saved. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_peter/1-5.htm

*Calvary Chapel*
- Chuck Smith: everything up to v. 5 is God's sovereign work, and "now he gets to your part," which is being kept through faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-peter/1-4.html

*Lutheran*
- 1517 tells preachers that vv. 3–9 are about assurance for people born again and receiving salvation. It stresses that Christ's resurrection actually does something, and points to 1 Peter 3:21–22. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-1-peter-13-9-easter-2-series-a-2026

**v. 9: what "salvation" means (Wesleyan holiness)**
- Wesley reads it as a present salvation "from all sin into all holiness." That fits his teaching on holiness, and it differs in emphasis from the Reformed sources above. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-peter-1.html
